displayQuote: I can think of no more stirring symbol of man's humanity to man than a fire engine

meta.title: Who really said "I can think of no more stirring symbol of man's humanity to man than a fire engine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Vonnegut wrote it — in The Sirens of Titan (1959). But the speaker is a character, Winston Niles Rumfoord, not Vonnegut himself.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I can think of no more stirring symbol of man's humanity to man than a fire engine'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Vonnegut’s writing, from The Sirens of Titan (1959) — though the words are put in a character’s mouth. He said his own version in 2001.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Vonnegut wrote it, in his second novel The Sirens of Titan (1959). One caveat the internet drops: it is dialogue. The line is spoken by Winston Niles Rumfoord, greeting Malachi Constant as he arrives on a volunteer fire department’s pumper. Vonnegut did say a version in his own voice — to the New York Post days after 9/11, using “fire truck.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Winston Niles Rumfoord — a character, not the author
Ch. 10, “An Age of Miracles”; p. 242 of the RosettaBooks electronic edition, p. 238 of the Easton Press (1990) printing

source.excerpt: “Welcome, Space Wanderer,” blatted Rumfoord’s oleomargarine tenor from the Gabriel horns on the wall. “How meet it is that you should come to us on the bright red pumper of a volunteer fire department. I can think of no more stirring symbol of man’s humanity to man than a fire engine. Tell me, Space Wanderer, do you see anything here—anything that makes you think you may have been here before?”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the line to The Sirens of Titan and reproduces the passage in full, identifying the speaker as Winston Niles Rumfoord.
Wikiquote’s sourced Vonnegut page ↗ independently lists the sentence under The Sirens of Titan (1959), ch. 10, “An Age of Miracles.”

Page numbers differ by printing, so we quote both that Quote Investigator verified ↗: p. 242 of 319 in the RosettaBooks electronic edition, and p. 238 of 315 in the Easton Press (1990) edition checked on paper.

Vonnegut said it again in his own voice. Quote Investigator records ↗ his comment to the New York Post of 17 September 2001: “The most stirring symbol of man’s humanity toward man that I can think of is a fire truck.”
source.excerptNote: Quoted alone, the sentence reads as Vonnegut’s own tribute to firefighters. In the novel it is said by Rumfoord, a rich, clairvoyant manipulator in the middle of staging a religion — so the warmth is doing double duty.

author.name: Kurt Vonnegut
author.heading: About Kurt Vonnegut
author.bio: Kurt Vonnegut (1922–2007) was an American novelist and essayist who survived the Allied firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war and spent the rest of his career writing about it, obliquely and then directly. Cat’s Cradle, Slaughterhouse-Five and Breakfast of Champions fused science fiction, black comedy and moral seriousness into a voice nobody has successfully imitated. In his last decades he wrote more essays than novels, and became one of the most quoted — and most misquoted — American writers on the internet.

misattribution.heading: Real Vonnegut — but not Vonnegut talking
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound; the framing usually is not. The line circulates as though Vonnegut were speaking in his own voice — the query that sent Quote Investigator looking came from a reader whose friend is a volunteer firefighter.

items.why: Vonnegut wrote the sentence, but a character says it. Quote Investigator ↗ makes the point plainly: “the pronouncements of a character in a novel do not always reflect the beliefs of the author.” Rumfoord is a manipulator mid-way through inventing a religion.

Some quotations render it “fire truck.” That is not a corruption of the novel — it is Vonnegut’s own later phrasing. Quote Investigator ↗ cites the New York Post of 17 September 2001: “The most stirring symbol of man’s humanity toward man that I can think of is a fire truck.”

The line travels the internet unsourced: the reader who put the question to Quote Investigator ↗ reported finding it on many sites and “not found any citation identifying when it was written or spoken.” There are two datable appearances, and both are QI’s: the 1959 novel ↗, and Vonnegut’s own remark to the New York Post in 2001.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: genuinely Vonnegut’s writing — The Sirens of Titan ↗, 1959 — with the caveat that the speaker is a character, and that Vonnegut’s own 2001 version said “fire truck.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Volunteer fire departments recur in Vonnegut’s work with a consistency that is hard to read as accidental. He treats them as the one institution humans have built that is unambiguously about running toward other people’s disasters for no reward — the opposite of everything his novels are usually satirising.

Quote Investigator notes the pattern beyond this line: in God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater (1965) the protagonist accidentally kills members of a volunteer fire department during the war and later pours a foundation’s money into supporting them. Whatever Rumfoord means by it, the author kept coming back to fire engines.
